claim: Sepsis is a common life-threatening condition caused by a deregulated host response to infection.
source: Sepsis is a common life-threatening condition caused by a deregulated host response to infection.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about sepsis that is presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Sepsis is characterized by profound systemic inflammation and disseminated intravascular coagulation, which often lead to multiple organ failure (MOF) and subsequent mortality.
source: This syndrome is characterized by profound systemic inflammation and disseminated intravascular coagulation, which often lead to multiple organ failure (MOF) and subsequent mortality (Singer et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Singer et al., 2016.

claim: The incidence of sepsis has risen by 9% to 13% annually.
source: The incidence of sepsis has risen by 9% to 13% annually, largely due to an expansion of the elderly population, more frequent invasive surgical procedures, and increased antibiotic resistance (Martin et al., 2003; Gaieski et al., 2013; Angus and Wax, 2001; Starr and Saito, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The rise in sepsis incidence is largely due to an expansion of the elderly population, more frequent invasive surgical procedures, and increased antibiotic resistance.
source: The incidence of sepsis has risen by 9% to 13% annually, largely due to an expansion of the elderly population, more frequent invasive surgical procedures, and increased antibiotic resistance (Martin et al., 2003; Gaieski et al., 2013; Angus and Wax, 2001; Starr and Saito, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Advances in critical care medicine and campaigns promoting early identification and treatment of sepsis have led to improved survival rates.
source: However, advances in critical care medicine and campaigns promoting early identification and treatment of sepsis have led to improved survival rates (Angus and Wax, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Angus and Wax, 2001.

claim: Nearly 1.5 million sepsis survivors are discharged annually from U.S. hospitals.
source: Consequently, nearly 1.5 million sepsis survivors are discharged annually from U.S. hospitals, approximately 14 million globally (Elixhauser et al., 2011; Prescott and Angus, 2018; Fleischmann et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Approximately 14 million sepsis survivors are discharged globally each year.
source: Consequently, nearly 1.5 million sepsis survivors are discharged annually from U.S. hospitals, approximately 14 million globally (Elixhauser et al., 2011; Prescott and Angus, 2018; Fleischmann et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Post-sepsis physical dysfunction exceeds that of intensive care unit acquired weakness (ICUAW) alone.
source: As the population of survivors grows, post-sepsis physical dysfunction, which exceeds that of intensive care unit acquired weakness (ICUAW) alone, has become a clear clinical problem (Prescott and Angus, 2018; Callahan and Supinski, 2009; Iwashyna et al., 2010; Schefold et al., 2010; Contrin et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Sepsis survivors rarely return to baseline functional status after discharge from the ICU.
source: Sepsis survivors rarely return to baseline functional status after discharge from the ICU.
evidence: This claim is presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Post-sepsis muscle weakness causes nearly half of previously functionally independent individuals to be discharged either to nursing care facilities or home with home care.
source: Post-sepsis muscle weakness causes nearly half of previously functionally independent individuals to be discharged either to nursing care facilities or home with home care (Odden et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Odden et al., 2013.

claim: Nearly a third of patients which were previously independent and had no prior comorbidities had problems with mobility one year after discharge.
source: Nearly a third of patients which were previously independent and had no prior comorbidities had problems with mobility one year after discharge (Yende et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yende et al., 2016.

claim: Survivors continue to develop functional limitations for at least 5 years following discharge, a trend that appears to be sepsis-specific.
source: Further, survivors continue to develop functional limitations for at least 5 years following discharge, a trend that appears to be sepsis-specific (Iwashyna et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Iwashyna et al., 2010.

claim: Less than half of previously employed individuals are able to return to work within one year after discharge.
source: Moreover, less than half of previously employed individuals are able to return to work within one year after discharge (Poulsen et al., 2009; Pettilä et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Poulsen et al., 2009 and Pettilä et al., 2000.

claim: The lack of an appropriate animal model has greatly impeded the identification of mechanisms that contribute to long-term dysfunction after sepsis.
source: Although post-sepsis muscle weakness is now widely recognized as a serious medical issue, the lack of an appropriate animal model has greatly impeded the identification of mechanisms that contribute to long-term dysfunction.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of research in the field.

claim: Current animal models of sepsis are either too severe, causing early death of most animals without recovery from sepsis, or too mild thus not triggering long-term chronic dysfunction.
source: Current animal models of sepsis are either too severe, causing early death of most animals without recovery from sepsis, or too mild thus not triggering long-term chronic dysfunction.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of existing animal models.

claim: The large majority of sepsis patients are late middle-age and older.
source: To further optimize our animal model for the current study, careful attention was also given to age, as the large majority of sepsis patients are late middle-age and older, and aging is an established risk factor for sepsis incidence, severity, and mortality (Angus and Wax, 2001; Starr and Saito, 2014; Elixhauser et al., 2011; Martin et al., 2006; Dombrovskiy et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Aging is an established risk factor for sepsis incidence, severity, and mortality.
source: To further optimize our animal model for the current study, careful attention was also given to age, as the large majority of sepsis patients are late middle-age and older, and aging is an established risk factor for sepsis incidence, severity, and mortality (Angus and Wax, 2001; Starr and Saito, 2014; Elixhauser et al., 2011; Martin et al., 2006; Dombrovskiy et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Sepsis survivors have significant skeletal muscle weakness for at least one month which cannot be attributed to muscle atrophy.
source: We show that sepsis survivors have significant skeletal muscle weakness for at least one month which cannot be attributed to muscle atrophy, but rather is associated with impaired mitochondrial activity and persistent protein oxidative damage.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Chronic muscle weakness in sepsis survivors is associated with impaired mitochondrial activity.
source: We show that sepsis survivors have significant skeletal muscle weakness for at least one month which cannot be attributed to muscle atrophy, but rather is associated with impaired mitochondrial activity and persistent protein oxidative damage.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Chronic muscle weakness in sepsis survivors is associated with persistent protein oxidative damage.
source: We show that sepsis survivors have significant skeletal muscle weakness for at least one month which cannot be attributed to muscle atrophy, but rather is associated with impaired mitochondrial activity and persistent protein oxidative damage.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The ICU-like sepsis model rescued 74.1% of middle-aged male mice from otherwise completely lethal (LD100) sepsis.
source: This protocol rescued 74.1% of middle-aged males from otherwise completely lethal (LD100) sepsis (Figure 1B, p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: No further mortality was observed after day 14 in the sepsis model.
source: No further mortality was observed after day 14.
evidence: This is an observation from the survival data.

claim: Resuscitation decreased bacterial load by day 2 in the sepsis model.
source: Assessment of bacteremia showed that resuscitation decreased bacterial load by day 2 (p=0.009), and resolved the systemic infection by day 4 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by bacteremia data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Resuscitation resolved the systemic infection by day 4 in the sepsis model.
source: Assessment of bacteremia showed that resuscitation decreased bacterial load by day 2 (p=0.009), and resolved the systemic infection by day 4 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by bacteremia data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 72.7% survival was achieved in middle-aged female mice compared to 16% survival without therapeutic intervention.
source: Similar data were obtained using middle-aged female mice: 72.7% survival was achieved compared to 16% survival without therapeutic intervention (Figure 1D, p=0.035), and bacteremia was rapidly resolved (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Male sepsis survivors had a 24.6% reduction in maximal specific force at 2 weeks compared to non-sepsis controls.
source: Compared to non-sepsis controls (NSC), male sepsis survivors had a 24.6% reduction in maximal specific force at 2 weeks (p<0.0001) and 17.4% reduction at 1 month (p=0.002, Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by muscle force data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Male sepsis survivors had a 17.4% reduction in maximal specific force at 1 month compared to non-sepsis controls.
source: Compared to non-sepsis controls (NSC), male sepsis survivors had a 24.6% reduction in maximal specific force at 2 weeks (p<0.0001) and 17.4% reduction at 1 month (p=0.002, Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by muscle force data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Female sepsis survivors were 19.8% weaker compared to controls at 2 weeks.
source: Similarly, female sepsis survivors were 19.8% weaker compared to controls at 2 weeks (p=0.035, Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by muscle force data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Sepsis-induced chronic muscle weakness could not be explained by atrophy since muscle force measurements are normalized to muscle size (physiological cross section).
source: Sepsis-induced chronic muscle weakness could not be explained by atrophy since muscle force measurements are normalized to muscle size (physiological cross section).
evidence: This is an inference based on the methodology used for muscle force measurements.

claim: Specific force was unchanged by resuscitation procedures (maximal force: 19.0 ± 0.8 N/cm2 in NSC vs 19.5 ± 0.8 N/cm2 in NSC + resuscitation, p=0.359).
source: We found that specific force was unchanged by resuscitation procedures (maximal force: 19.0 ± 0.8 N/cm2 in NSC vs 19.5 ± 0.8 N/cm2 in NSC + resuscitation, p=0.359).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing NSC and NSC + resuscitation groups.

claim: Plasma IL-6 concentration was elevated at day 4 but comparable to NSC by 2 weeks in both male and female sepsis survivors.
source: Despite resolution of bacteremia, plasma IL-6 concentration was elevated at day 4 (p<0.0001), but comparable to NSC by 2 weeks in both male and female sepsis survivors (p=0.999 and p=0.667, respectively, Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by cytokine data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Gene expression of IL-6 and TNFα in gastrocnemius muscle were comparable among NSC and sepsis survivors at 2 weeks.
source: Likewise, gene expression of these cytokines in gastrocnemius muscle showed that pro-inflammatory IL-6 (Figure 2D) and TNFα (Figure 2E) were comparable among NSC and sepsis survivors at 2 weeks (p=0.622 and p=0.565, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figures 2D and 2E.

claim: Muscle weakness is not associated with ongoing systemic or local muscle inflammation.
source: These data indicate that muscle weakness is not associated with ongoing systemic or local muscle inflammation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cytokine and gene expression data.

claim: IL-10, an anti-inflammatory cytokine, was 2.5-fold higher in sepsis survivors compared to NSC.
source: Interestingly, IL-10, an anti-inflammatory cytokine, was 2.5-fold higher in sepsis survivors compared to NSC (p=0.011, Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Splenomegaly was observed in many sepsis animals on day 4 (males, 76.4% larger, p=0.0003 compared to NSC).
source: In addition, we observed splenomegaly in many sepsis animals on day 4 (males, 76.4% larger, p=0.0003 compared to NSC) which remained elevated at 2 weeks (males, 49.7% larger, p=0.004; females 20.2% larger, p=0.034), but recovered by 1 month (males p=0.905, Figure 2G,H) which may be indicative of high antigen clearance during recovery from sepsis (Bronte and Pittet, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by spleen weight data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Splenomegaly remained elevated at 2 weeks (males, 49.7% larger, p=0.004; females 20.2% larger, p=0.034).
source: In addition, we observed splenomegaly in many sepsis animals on day 4 (males, 76.4% larger, p=0.0003 compared to NSC) which remained elevated at 2 weeks (males, 49.7% larger, p=0.004; females 20.2% larger, p=0.034), but recovered by 1 month (males p=0.905, Figure 2G,H) which may be indicative of high antigen clearance during recovery from sepsis (Bronte and Pittet, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by spleen weight data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Splenomegaly recovered by 1 month (males p=0.905).
source: In addition, we observed splenomegaly in many sepsis animals on day 4 (males, 76.4% larger, p=0.0003 compared to NSC) which remained elevated at 2 weeks (males, 49.7% larger, p=0.004; females 20.2% larger, p=0.034), but recovered by 1 month (males p=0.905, Figure 2G,H) which may be indicative of high antigen clearance during recovery from sepsis (Bronte and Pittet, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by spleen weight data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Middle-aged sepsis survivors exhibit chronic muscle weakness, even after bacteremia and systemic inflammation are resolved.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that middle-aged sepsis survivors exhibit chronic muscle weakness, even after bacteremia and systemic inflammation are resolved.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data presented in the Results section.

claim: Animals with sepsis lost significant body weight over time (males p=0.003 compared to NSC).
source: Animals with sepsis lost significant body weight over time (males p=0.003 compared to NSC, Figure 3A; females p=0.001, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Analyses of body composition by EchoMRI revealed a significant loss of fat mass after sepsis induction (p=0.004 compared to NSC).
source: Analyses of body composition by EchoMRI revealed a significant loss of fat mass after sepsis induction (p=0.004 compared to NSC, Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by body composition data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Loss of lean mass was observed during the first 5 days (p=0.005 compared to NSC) which steadily recovered thereafter and became comparable to non-sepsis controls by two weeks (p=0.821).
source: On the other hand, loss of lean mass was observed during the first 5 days (p=0.005 compared to NSC) which steadily recovered thereafter and became comparable to non-sepsis controls by two weeks (p=0.821, Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by body composition data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Body weight remained significantly lower than baseline 1 month post-sepsis (6.12% lower, p<0.0001).
source: In a selected experiment in which sepsis survivors were kept 1 month post-sepsis, body weight remained significantly lower than baseline (6.12% lower, p<0.0001, data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data, though the data are not shown in the manuscript.

claim: Sustained weight loss in murine sepsis survivors is attributable to loss of fat mass, not lean mass.
source: These results suggest that sustained weight loss in murine sepsis survivors is attributable to loss of fat mass, not lean mass.
evidence: This is an inference based on the body composition data.

claim: The wet weight of the predominantly fast-glycolytic muscles tibialis anterior (TA) and extensor digitorum longus (EDL), and the mixed fiber-type gastrocnemius (GA) were reduced at day 4 compared to non-sepsis controls.
source: The wet weight of the predominantly fast-glycolytic muscles tibialis anterior (TA) and extensor digitorum longus (EDL), and the mixed fiber-type gastrocnemius (GA) were reduced at day 4 compared to non-sepsis controls (p=0.054, p<0.0001, and p=0.001, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by muscle wet weight data.

claim: The wet weight of TA, EDL, and GA muscles was lower at 2 weeks and was comparable to non-sepsis controls at 1 month.
source: The wet weight of these muscles was lower at 2 weeks and was comparable to non-sepsis controls at 1 month (p=0.918 for EDL and p=0.242 for GA).
evidence: This claim is supported by muscle wet weight data.

claim: Changes in muscle size were proportional to loss of body weight as evidenced by skeletal muscle weight to body weight ratio.
source: While these data are indicative of muscle loss, it is important to note that changes in muscle size were proportional to loss of body weight as evidenced by skeletal muscle weight to body weight ratio (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by muscle weight to body weight ratio data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The mean CSA of fast-twitch (type II) fibers showed sepsis-mediated atrophy on day 4 (IIa p=0.023, IIb p=0.044, and IIx p=0.0034) which was largely recovered by 2 weeks.
source: The mean CSA of fast-twitch (type II) fibers showed sepsis-mediated atrophy on day 4 (IIa p=0.023, IIb p=0.044, and IIx p=0.0034) which was largely recovered by 2 weeks, whereas little, if any, atrophy was observed in slow (type I) fibers (p=0.626).
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-sectional area analysis data.

claim: Little, if any, atrophy was observed in slow (type I) fibers (p=0.626).
source: The mean CSA of fast-twitch (type II) fibers showed sepsis-mediated atrophy on day 4 (IIa p=0.023, IIb p=0.044, and IIx p=0.0034) which was largely recovered by 2 weeks, whereas little, if any, atrophy was observed in slow (type I) fibers (p=0.626).
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-sectional area analysis data.

claim: Analysis of the predominantly slow-oxidative soleus muscle did not reveal sepsis-induced atrophy (type I fibers p=0.521, IIa p=0.799).
source: Analysis of the predominantly slow-oxidative soleus muscle did not reveal sepsis-induced atrophy (type I fibers p=0.521, IIa p=0.799, Figure 3—figure supplement 2) which is consistent with the wet weight (Figure 3D, right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-sectional area analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Preferential atrophy of fast-twitch fibers occurs during critical illness.
source: These data are consistent with clinical reports which show that preferential atrophy of fast-twitch fibers occurs during critical illness (Gutmann et al., 1996; Bierbrauer et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical reports.

claim: Chronic muscle weakness in murine sepsis survivors cannot be attributed to muscle wasting alone.
source: Collectively, these data provide evidence that chronic muscle weakness in murine sepsis survivors cannot be attributed to muscle wasting alone.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing muscle recovery but persistent weakness.

claim: A long-term reduction in muscle function of murine sepsis survivors must be largely attributable to impaired quality, rather than quantity.
source: Therefore, a long-term reduction in muscle function of murine sepsis survivors must be largely attributable to impaired quality, rather than quantity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing muscle recovery but persistent weakness.

claim: Skeletal muscle mitochondrial dysfunction is evident during ICU stay in sepsis patients.
source: In sepsis patients, skeletal muscle mitochondrial dysfunction is evident during their stay in the ICU (Fredriksson et al., 2006; Fredriksson et al., 2008), but it is unknown whether such mitochondrial derangements persist after recovery from sepsis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fredriksson et al., 2006 and 2008.

claim: It is unknown whether mitochondrial derangements persist after recovery from sepsis.
source: In sepsis patients, skeletal muscle mitochondrial dysfunction is evident during their stay in the ICU (Fredriksson et al., 2006; Fredriksson et al., 2008), but it is unknown whether such mitochondrial derangements persist after recovery from sepsis.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: Normal mitochondrial morphology in non-sepsis controls is characterized by highly organized lamellar cristae.
source: Normal mitochondrial morphology was evident in non-sepsis controls characterized by highly organized lamellar cristae (i.e.inner mitochondrial membrane arranged in parallel stacks).
evidence: This is a description of the control group observations from TEM analysis.

claim: Striking morphological alterations were observed frequently in both IMF mitochondria and SS mitochondria in muscle from sepsis survivors.
source: On the other hand, striking morphological alterations were observed frequently in both IMF mitochondria and SS mitochondria in muscle from sepsis survivors.
evidence: This is a description of the sepsis survivor group observations from TEM analysis.

claim: Numerous mitochondria with fragmented cristae and enlarged matrix space were observed in the muscles from sepsis survivors.
source: Even observation at low magnification (5,000X) revealed numerous mitochondria with fragmented cristae and enlarged matrix space in the muscles from sepsis survivors.
evidence: This is a description of the sepsis survivor group observations from TEM analysis.

claim: Some mitochondria in sepsis survivors were nearly devoid of cristae.
source: These features are better appreciated at higher magnification (15,000X) by which we also observed some mitochondria nearly devoid of cristae, 'onion-like' concentric swirling of cristae (Jiang et al., 2017; Walker and Benzer, 2004), as well as compartmentalization in vesicle-like structures (Sun et al., 2007; Vincent et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a description of the sepsis survivor group observations from TEM analysis.

claim: 'Onion-like' concentric swirling of cristae was observed in mitochondria from sepsis survivors.
source: These features are better appreciated at higher magnification (15,000X) by which we also observed some mitochondria nearly devoid of cristae, 'onion-like' concentric swirling of cristae (Jiang et al., 2017; Walker and Benzer, 2004), as well as compartmentalization in vesicle-like structures (Sun et al., 2007; Vincent et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a description of the sepsis survivor group observations from TEM analysis, with citations to prior literature describing similar features.

claim: Compartmentalization in vesicle-like structures was observed in mitochondria from sepsis survivors.
source: These features are better appreciated at higher magnification (15,000X) by which we also observed some mitochondria nearly devoid of cristae, 'onion-like' concentric swirling of cristae (Jiang et al., 2017; Walker and Benzer, 2004), as well as compartmentalization in vesicle-like structures (Sun et al., 2007; Vincent et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a description of the sepsis survivor group observations from TEM analysis, with citations to prior literature describing similar features.

claim: Normal mitochondria made up a significantly smaller proportion of the total IMF mitochondria in sepsis survivors (p=0.002).
source: Normal mitochondria made up a significantly smaller proportion of the total IMF (Figure 4D) and SS (Figure 4E) mitochondria in sepsis survivors (p=0.002 and p=0.048, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphometric analysis data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Normal mitochondria made up a significantly smaller proportion of the total SS mitochondria in sepsis survivors (p=0.048).
source: Normal mitochondria made up a significantly smaller proportion of the total IMF (Figure 4D) and SS (Figure 4E) mitochondria in sepsis survivors (p=0.002 and p=0.048, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphometric analysis data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: IMF mitochondria were seemingly more affected in the post-sepsis condition, where aberrant and empty mitochondria represented a significantly larger proportion of the mitochondria (p=0.029 and 0.049, respectively) compared to controls.
source: IMF mitochondria were seemingly more affected in the post-sepsis condition, where aberrant and empty mitochondria represented a significantly larger proportion of the mitochondria (p=0.029 and 0.049, respectively) compared to controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by morphometric analysis data.

claim: The maximal ADP phosphorylation rate (State III) was significantly lower (27.3% p=0.003) in sepsis survivors compared to that of controls.
source: These results showed that the maximal ADP phosphorylation rate (State III) and Complex I-driven electron transport (State V-CI) were significantly lower (27.3% p=0.003, and 26.6% p=0.017, respectively) in sepsis survivors compared to that of controls (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by mitochondrial respiration data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Complex I-driven electron transport (State V-CI) was significantly lower (26.6% p=0.017) in sepsis survivors compared to that of controls.
source: These results showed that the maximal ADP phosphorylation rate (State III) and Complex I-driven electron transport (State V-CI) were significantly lower (27.3% p=0.003, and 26.6% p=0.017, respectively) in sepsis survivors compared to that of controls (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by mitochondrial respiration data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Complex II-driven maximum electron transport (State V-CII) showed a non-significant (p=0.099) trend of lower OCR in sepsis survivors.
source: On the other hand, Complex II-driven maximum electron transport (State V-CII) showed a non-significant (p=0.099) trend of lower OCR in sepsis survivors (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by mitochondrial respiration data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Skeletal muscle mitochondria in sepsis survivors have significantly reduced mitochondrial bioenergetics.
source: These results show that skeletal muscle mitochondria in sepsis survivors have significantly reduced mitochondrial bioenergetics.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the mitochondrial respiration data.

claim: On the first day of sepsis, animals ate only 11.08% of their baseline (0.52 g compared to 5.19 g; p<0.001).
source: On the first day of sepsis, animals ate only 11.08% of their baseline (0.52 g compared to 5.19 g; p<0.001), which steadily increased to 75.51% by day 4 (3.53 g, p=0.042) and returned to near-baseline thereafter.
evidence: This claim is supported by food consumption data.

claim: Food consumption steadily increased to 75.51% by day 4 (3.53 g, p=0.042) and returned to near-baseline thereafter.
source: On the first day of sepsis, animals ate only 11.08% of their baseline (0.52 g compared to 5.19 g; p<0.001), which steadily increased to 75.51% by day 4 (3.53 g, p=0.042) and returned to near-baseline thereafter.
evidence: This claim is supported by food consumption data.

claim: Oxygen consumption rate (OCR) was similar among pair-fed and freely-fed mice (State III p=0.944, State V-CI p=0.737, State V-CII p=0.185).
source: Oxygen consumption rate (OCR) was measured in isolated mitochondria from the TA which showed similar mitochondrial respiration capacity among pair-fed and freely-fed mice (State III p=0.944, State V-CI p=0.737, State V-CII p=0.185; Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by mitochondrial respiration data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The reduced food intake during sepsis does not contribute to chronic mitochondrial impairment in sepsis surviving mice.
source: These data confirm that the reduced food intake during sepsis does not contribute to chronic mitochondrial impairment in sepsis surviving mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pair-feeding experiment data.

claim: Complex I activity (measured by NADH) was 22.2% lower at day 4 and 40.8% lower at 2 weeks compared to NSC, although statistical significance was not achieved.
source: Quantification of stain intensities was conducted (Figure 6B) which showed that complex I activity (measured by nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide dehydrogenase (NADH), Figure 6A, top row) was 22.2% lower at day 4% and 40.8% lower at 2 weeks compared to NSC, although statistical significance was not achieved.
evidence: This claim is supported by histochemical staining data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Complex II activity (measured by SDH) was 19.8% lower at day 4 and 38.1% lower at 2 weeks (p=0.015).
source: Complex II activity (measured by succinate dehydrogenase (SDH), Figure 6A, middle row) was 19.8% lower at day 4% and 38.1% lower at 2 weeks (p=0.015).
evidence: This claim is supported by histochemical staining data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Overall mitochondrial respiration activity assessed by cytochrome c oxidase staining (COX; complex IV) was 43.7% lower at day 4 (p<0.001) and 48.6% lower at 2 weeks (p<0.001).
source: Overall mitochondrial respiration activity was assessed by cytochrome c oxidase staining (COX; complex IV; Figure 6A, bottom row) which was 43.7% lower at day 4 (p<0.001) and 48.6% lower at 2 weeks (p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by histochemical staining data shown in Figure 6.

claim: 2 weeks after sepsis some myofibers had areas devoid of staining which was consistent among serial sections for the different mitochondrial enzyme activities.
source: Interestingly, 2 weeks after sepsis some myofibers had areas devoid of staining which was consistent among serial sections for the different mitochondrial enzyme activities (Figure 6, right column, yellow arrows).
evidence: This is an observation from the histochemical staining data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The areas devoid of mitochondrial enzyme activity were not devoid of tissue.
source: Using hematoxylin and eosin stained serial sections we confirmed that the areas devoid of mitochondrial enzyme activity were not devoid of tissue.
evidence: This is a confirmation based on H&E staining.

claim: The areas devoid of histochemical staining in the myofibers of sepsis survivors are likely the areas that house 'empty' or highly 'aberrant' mitochondria as depicted by TEM analysis.
source: We hypothesize that the areas devoid of histochemical staining in the myofibers of sepsis survivors (Figure 6A, right column) are likely the areas that house 'empty' or highly 'aberrant' mitochondria as depicted in Figure 4 by TEM analysis.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the integration of histochemical and TEM data.

claim: Mitochondrial complex enzyme activities are impaired long after sepsis itself is resolved.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that mitochondrial complex enzyme activities are impaired long after sepsis itself is resolved.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the histochemical staining data.

claim: Complex I-driven respiration seems more affected than Complex II-driven activity as evidenced by respiration analysis in isolated mitochondria.
source: Complex I-driven respiration seems more affected than Complex II-driven activity as evidenced by respiration analysis in isolated mitochondria (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an inference based on the mitochondrial respiration data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Histochemical analysis indicated that CII-driven activity is also significantly affected in the post-sepsis condition.
source: However, histochemical analysis, which reflects mitochondrial bioenergetics in whole tissue, indicated that CII-driven activity is also significantly affected in the post-sepsis condition (Figure 6).
evidence: This is an inference based on the histochemical staining data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Significant production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reactive nitrogen species (RNS) is triggered during sepsis due to inflammation, tissue hypoxia, and mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: Significant production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reactive nitrogen species (RNS) is triggered during sepsis due to inflammation, tissue hypoxia (Ueda et al., 2008; Starr et al., 2011), and mitochondrial dysfunction (Fredriksson et al., 2006; Zolfaghari et al., 2015; Singer, 2014; Castello et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Carbonylation was detected in proteins ranging in size from ~37 to 250 kDa, and showed ~2 fold higher levels in sepsis survivors at 2 weeks (p=0.002).
source: Carbonylation was detected in proteins ranging in size from ~37 to 250 kDa, and showed ~2 fold higher levels in sepsis survivors at 2 weeks, as quantified by densitometric analysis of the entire lane (p=0.002, Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Carbonylation trend was no longer evident at 1 month (p=0.832).
source: This trend was no longer evident at 1 month (p=0.832, Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: 3-nitrotyrosine was ~2.5 fold higher in muscle from 2 week sepsis survivors (p=0.016).
source: Multiple bands were also detected with the oxidative marker 3-nitrotyrosine, which was ~2.5 fold higher in muscle from 2 week sepsis survivors (p=0.016, Figure 7C) which remained modestly elevated at 1 month (p=0.099, Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: 3-nitrotyrosine remained modestly elevated at 1 month (p=0.099).
source: Multiple bands were also detected with the oxidative marker 3-nitrotyrosine, which was ~2.5 fold higher in muscle from 2 week sepsis survivors (p=0.016, Figure 7C) which remained modestly elevated at 1 month (p=0.099, Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Sepsis survivors have significant oxidative and nitro-oxidative damage even long after the acute sepsis condition has passed.
source: These results demonstrate that sepsis survivors have significant oxidative and nitro-oxidative damage even long after the acute sepsis condition has passed, which may indicate that (1) damage is not successfully cleared and therefore persists in the post-sepsis condition, and/or (2) damage is potentially propagated continuously by impaired mitochondrial activity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the oxidative damage data.

claim: Damage is not successfully cleared and therefore persists in the post-sepsis condition.
source: These results demonstrate that sepsis survivors have significant oxidative and nitro-oxidative damage even long after the acute sepsis condition has passed, which may indicate that (1) damage is not successfully cleared and therefore persists in the post-sepsis condition, and/or (2) damage is potentially propagated continuously by impaired mitochondrial activity.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the oxidative damage data.

claim: Damage is potentially propagated continuously by impaired mitochondrial activity.
source: These results demonstrate that sepsis survivors have significant oxidative and nitro-oxidative damage even long after the acute sepsis condition has passed, which may indicate that (1) damage is not successfully cleared and therefore persists in the post-sepsis condition, and/or (2) damage is potentially propagated continuously by impaired mitochondrial activity.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the oxidative damage data.

claim: This is the first study to demonstrate skeletal muscle dysfunction long after recovery from experimental sepsis.
source: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to demonstrate skeletal muscle dysfunction long after recovery from experimental sepsis.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: Murine sepsis survivors have prolonged muscle weakness, independent of muscle atrophy, that is associated with ongoing mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative damage.
source: We show that murine sepsis survivors have prolonged muscle weakness, independent of muscle atrophy, that is associated with ongoing mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative damage.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Patients at late middle-age more frequently suffer from post-sepsis dysfunction due to confounding issues such as preexisting comorbidities, reduced muscle mass, and lower protein intake.
source: First, in addition to being more likely to develop sepsis (Starr and Saito, 2014; Elixhauser et al., 2011; Dombrovskiy et al., 2007), patients at late middle-age more frequently suffer from post-sepsis dysfunction due to confounding issues such as preexisting comorbidities, reduced muscle mass, and lower protein intake (Contrin et al., 2013; Rahman et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Late middle-age patients are most vulnerable to economic repercussions since post-sepsis functional limitations often prevent them from returning to work.
source: Further, these patients are most vulnerable to economic repercussions since post-sepsis functional limitations often prevent them from returning to work (Iwashyna et al., 2012; Hofhuis et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Patients who survived septic shock had reduced physical functioning and general health compared to patients who survived uncomplicated sepsis or sterile systemic inflammatory response syndrome.
source: Battle and colleagues (Battle et al., 2014) reported that patients who survived septic shock had reduced physical functioning and general health compared to patients who survived uncomplicated sepsis or sterile (i.e. non-infectious) systemic inflammatory response syndrome.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Battle et al., 2014.

claim: Animal models of sepsis with mild or modest severity have little clinical relevance.
source: Likewise, this suggests that animal models of sepsis with mild or modest severity (i.e. no to little mortality in the absence of resuscitation) have little clinical relevance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the clinical data cited.

claim: Experimental sepsis should be severe enough to cause chronic dysfunction.
source: In order to model the morbidities with which sepsis survivors present clinically, experimental sepsis should be severe enough to cause chronic dysfunction, as we demonstrate in the present study.
evidence: This is a methodological claim based on the authors' reasoning.

claim: Limited research that has been conducted at later time-points after experimental sepsis did not include muscle function assessment in parallel with molecular analyses.
source: Third, the limited research that has been conducted at later time-points after experimental sepsis did not include muscle function assessment in parallel with molecular analyses, thus actual muscle weakness was not confirmed.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of prior research.

claim: In the CLP animal model, surgical complications may influence recovery.
source: Fourth, many sepsis studies use the CLP animal model; however, in this model surgical complications may influence recovery.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the CLP model.

claim: Differences in cecum shape and size among older mice lead to inconsistency in ligation site in the CLP model.
source: Further, differences in cecum shape and size among older mice lead to inconsistency in ligation site (Starr et al., 2014), and in mice kept long-term, the ligated cecum may result in unresolved necrosis, and sustained inflammation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Starr et al., 2014.

claim: In mice kept long-term, the ligated cecum may result in unresolved necrosis, and sustained inflammation.
source: Further, differences in cecum shape and size among older mice lead to inconsistency in ligation site (Starr et al., 2014), and in mice kept long-term, the ligated cecum may result in unresolved necrosis, and sustained inflammation.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the CLP model.

claim: This model mimics the clinical situation since aged subjects are most at risk for sepsis incidence, morbidity, and mortality.
source: Thus, this model mimics the clinical situation since aged subjects are most at risk for sepsis incidence, morbidity, and mortality.
evidence: This is a claim about the clinical relevance of the model.

claim: This long-term model replicates the clinical presentation of post sepsis syndrome, or the broader issue of post-intensive care syndrome (PICS), in which the patient survives but remains physically weak, even in the absence of muscle wasting.
source: Additionally, this long-term model replicates the clinical presentation of post sepsis syndrome, or the broader issue of post-intensive care syndrome (PICS), in which the patient survives but remains physically weak, even in the absence of muscle wasting.
evidence: This is a claim about the clinical relevance of the model.

claim: Prevention of muscle wasting is a large clinical focus.
source: This differentiation between quality vs quantity is highly important, as prevention of muscle wasting is a large clinical focus (Cohen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cohen et al., 2015.

claim: Muscle wasting is a major concern for sepsis patients in the ICU.
source: Muscle wasting is a major concern for sepsis patients in the ICU.
evidence: This is a statement about the clinical context.

claim: Numerous factors, most notably muscle unloading during bedrest, insufficient nutrition, pharmacologic exposures, and imbalanced protein catabolism and synthesis, have been shown to contribute to sepsis-mediated atrophy.
source: Numerous factors, most notably muscle unloading during bedrest, insufficient nutrition, pharmacologic exposures, and imbalanced protein catabolism and synthesis, have been shown to contribute to sepsis-mediated atrophy (Schefold et al., 2010; Schreiber et al., 2018; Eikermann et al., 2006; Spranger et al., 2003; Dres et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2018; Lang et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2018; Vary and Kimball, 1992; Puthucheary et al., 2013; Bouglé et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Clinical interventions with early mobilization and nutritional support have not improved long-term outcomes.
source: However, clinical interventions with early mobilization (Denehy et al., 2013; Morris et al., 2016; Moss et al., 2016; Tipping et al., 2017) and nutritional support (Goossens et al., 2017; Hermans et al., 2013; Ogilvie and Larsson, 2014) have not improved long-term outcomes, and some studies even show negative effects of high protein delivery on muscle wasting (Puthucheary et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Some studies show negative effects of high protein delivery on muscle wasting.
source: However, clinical interventions with early mobilization (Denehy et al., 2013; Morris et al., 2016; Moss et al., 2016; Tipping et al., 2017) and nutritional support (Goossens et al., 2017; Hermans et al., 2013; Ogilvie and Larsson, 2014) have not improved long-term outcomes, and some studies even show negative effects of high protein delivery on muscle wasting (Puthucheary et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Puthucheary et al., 2013.

claim: Muscle weakness is not always accompanied by muscle wasting: they are separate entities that should not be considered synonymously.
source: Beyond this key issue, muscle weakness is not always accompanied by muscle wasting: they are separate entities that should not be considered synonymously (Schefold et al., 2010; Reid and Moylan, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Schefold et al., 2010 and Reid and Moylan, 2011.

claim: Therapeutic targets beyond muscle wasting are more likely to improve post-sepsis muscle weakness.
source: Nonetheless, taken together our data suggest therapeutic targets beyond muscle wasting are more likely to improve post-sepsis muscle weakness.
evidence: This is an inference based on the study's findings.

claim: Mitochondrial damage may be a key driver of chronic muscle weakness in murine sepsis survivors.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that mitochondrial damage may be a key driver of chronic muscle weakness in murine sepsis survivors.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: Healthy mitochondria are critical for efficient muscle function, an ATP-dependent process.
source: Healthy mitochondria are critical for efficient muscle function, an ATP-dependent process.
evidence: This is a statement of established biological knowledge.

claim: Skeletal muscles are mitochondrial dense and heavy oxygen consumers and thus greatly susceptible to damage during hypoxic conditions, including sepsis.
source: Skeletal muscles are mitochondrial dense and heavy oxygen consumers and thus greatly susceptible to damage during hypoxic conditions, including sepsis (Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhou et al., 2014.

claim: The IMF mitochondria, which are primarily responsible for ATP production for muscle contraction, are more significantly damaged than SS mitochondria.
source: Notably, the IMF mitochondria, which are primarily responsible for ATP production for muscle contraction (Hood, 2001; Timpani et al., 2015), are more significantly damaged than SS mitochondria.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, with citations supporting the role of IMF mitochondria.

claim: Mitochondrial structure and function are tightly linked.
source: As has been described (Vincent et al., 2016), mitochondrial structure and function are tightly linked; thus, derangements are associated with profound physiological implications.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vincent et al., 2016.

claim: The loss of inner mitochondrial membrane, as well as the abnormal presence of concentric/swirling cristae likely cause reduced bioenergetics in the post-sepsis condition.
source: The loss of inner mitochondrial membrane (where oxidative phosphorylation occurs), as well as the abnormal presence of concentric/swirling cristae likely cause reduced bioenergetics in the post-sepsis condition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations and known mitochondrial biology.

claim: In some myofibers there are areas devoid of any functional mitochondrial enzyme activity, where mitochondria are not capable of converting energy substrates to detectable levels.
source: We also unexpectedly found that in some myofibers there are areas devoid of any functional mitochondrial enzyme activity, where mitochondria are not capable of converting energy substrates to detectable levels.
evidence: This is a finding from the histochemical analysis.

claim: Such mitochondrial impairments would contribute to reduced muscle contraction.
source: As muscle contraction is dependent on ATP for cross-bridge cycling, one can conclude that such mitochondrial impairments would contribute to reduced muscle contraction.
evidence: This is an inference based on known muscle physiology.

claim: Accumulation of grossly damaged and dysfunctional mitochondria in middle-aged sepsis survivors is likely perpetuated by the fact that mitophagy decreases during aging.
source: It is important to note that accumulation of such grossly damaged and dysfunctional mitochondria in middle-aged sepsis survivors is likely perpetuated by the fact that mitophagy decreases during aging (Sun et al., 2007; Jang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sun et al., 2007 and Jang et al., 2018.

claim: Damaged mitochondria result in reduced ATP synthesis and increased oxidative stress.
source: Damaged mitochondria not only result in reduced ATP synthesis, but also in increased oxidative stress.
evidence: This is a statement of established biological knowledge.

claim: Mitochondria generate superoxide anions and nitric oxide as a byproduct of oxidative phosphorylation.
source: As a byproduct of oxidative phosphorylation, mitochondria generate superoxide anions and nitric oxide.
evidence: This is a statement of established biological knowledge.

claim: Mitochondrial damage, especially to complex I, triggers persistent production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reactive nitrogen species (RNS).
source: Mitochondrial damage, especially to complex I (Castello et al., 2006), triggers persistent production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reactive nitrogen species (RNS) (Balaban et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Castello et al., 2006 and Balaban et al., 2005.

claim: Sarcomeric proteins, including tropomyosin, actin, and creatine kinase, scavenge free radicals during oxidative stress which causes post-translational modifications.
source: Previous studies have shown that sarcomeric proteins, including tropomyosin, actin, and creatine kinase, scavenge free radicals during oxidative stress which causes post-translational modifications (Fedorova et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fedorova et al., 2009.

claim: Oxidative modifications are irreversible and require protein turnover for elimination.
source: Importantly, these oxidative modifications are irreversible (Cai and Yan, 2013) and require protein turnover for elimination.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cai and Yan, 2013.

claim: Oxidative stress has been shown to directly cause muscle fatigue.
source: As oxidative stress has been shown to directly cause muscle fatigue (Shindoh et al., 1990; Reid, 2008; Stasko et al., 2013), our data suggest that persistent oxidative stress in the post-sepsis condition likely contributes to chronic muscle weakness.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Shindoh et al., 1990, Reid, 2008, and Stasko et al., 2013.

claim: Persistent oxidative stress in the post-sepsis condition likely contributes to chronic muscle weakness.
source: As oxidative stress has been shown to directly cause muscle fatigue (Shindoh et al., 1990; Reid, 2008; Stasko et al., 2013), our data suggest that persistent oxidative stress in the post-sepsis condition likely contributes to chronic muscle weakness.
evidence: This is an inference based on the oxidative damage data and cited literature.

claim: The ROS and RNS secreted as a result of sepsis-induced mitochondrial damage then likely propagate mitochondrial dysfunction and energy failure through inhibition of the electron transport chain, thus acting as a vicious cycle of damage and functional decline.
source: Moreover, the ROS and RNS secreted as a result of sepsis-induced mitochondrial damage then likely propagate mitochondrial dysfunction and energy failure through inhibition of the electron transport chain, thus acting as a vicious cycle of damage and functional decline (Harman, 1972; Brandt et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Harman, 1972 and Brandt et al., 2017.

claim: Profound weakness is present in the skeletal muscle of murine sepsis survivors.
source: In summary, the present study demonstrates that profound weakness is present in the skeletal muscle of murine sepsis survivors and that such muscle weakness is not attributed to loss of muscle quantity alone, but rather is characterized by impaired quality on the mitochondrial and myofibrillar levels.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Muscle weakness is not attributed to loss of muscle quantity alone, but rather is characterized by impaired quality on the mitochondrial and myofibrillar levels.
source: In summary, the present study demonstrates that profound weakness is present in the skeletal muscle of murine sepsis survivors and that such muscle weakness is not attributed to loss of muscle quantity alone, but rather is characterized by impaired quality on the mitochondrial and myofibrillar levels.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Significant mitochondrial damage and dysfunction, as well as marked oxidative damage to skeletal muscle proteins, together likely contribute to chronic muscle weakness in sepsis survivors.
source: Significant mitochondrial damage and dysfunction, as well as marked oxidative damage to skeletal muscle proteins, together likely contribute to chronic muscle weakness in sepsis survivors.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Mitochondrial dysfunction is central to other altered muscle physiology in the post-sepsis state, such as redox balance, calcium homeostasis, repressed autophagy, and mitochondrial permeability transition pore opening.
source: We propose that mitochondrial dysfunction is central to other altered muscle physiology in the post-sepsis state, such as redox balance, calcium homeostasis, repressed autophagy, and mitochondrial permeability transition pore opening, altogether largely contributing to post-sepsis muscle weakness.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the study's findings.

claim: Therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring mitochondrial health, in addition to restoring muscle mass, will likely allow survivors to regain strength and improve quality of life after sepsis.
source: This work provides strong evidence that therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring mitochondrial health, in addition to restoring muscle mass, will likely allow survivors to regain strength and improve quality of life after sepsis.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: Sustained mitochondrial dysfunction, rather than atrophy alone, underlies chronic sepsis-induced muscle weakness.
source: Our data suggest that sustained mitochondrial dysfunction, rather than atrophy alone, underlies chronic sepsis-induced muscle weakness.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the abstract.

claim: Conventional efforts that aim to recover muscle quantity will likely remain ineffective for regaining strength and improving quality of life after sepsis until deficiencies in muscle quality are addressed.
source: This study emphasizes that conventional efforts that aim to recover muscle quantity will likely remain ineffective for regaining strength and improving quality of life after sepsis until deficiencies in muscle quality are addressed.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion from the abstract.

claim: Abnormal mitochondrial ultrastructure was evident in the muscle of survivors.
source: Abnormal mitochondrial ultrastructure, impaired respiration and electron transport chain activities, and persistent protein oxidative damage were evident in the muscle of survivors.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the abstract.

claim: Impaired respiration and electron transport chain activities were evident in the muscle of survivors.
source: Abnormal mitochondrial ultrastructure, impaired respiration and electron transport chain activities, and persistent protein oxidative damage were evident in the muscle of survivors.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the abstract.

claim: Persistent protein oxidative damage was evident in the muscle of survivors.
source: Abnormal mitochondrial ultrastructure, impaired respiration and electron transport chain activities, and persistent protein oxidative damage were evident in the muscle of survivors.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the abstract.
